title: Labbayk, O God, Labbayk
summary: Editorial timed to the closing day of Hajj 1447, drawing on the pilgrim's talbiyah to argue that tawhid is the central purpose for which all prophets were sent. The piece presents Hajj as the most concentrated ritual expression of tawhid, then extends the claim, arguing that authentic monotheism requires not only worship but active disavowal of and combat against 'polytheists' and 'tyrants'. It identifies Iran (framed as 'the Iranian tyranny') and the United States as principal enemies of tawhid and frames the group's armed campaign as the practical continuation of the prophetic mission. The talbiyah is repurposed as a metaphor for fighter dedication and enlistment. Quranic citations and a hadith attributed to Bukhari anchor the argument in classical textual authority. The text is thematic and exhortative rather than operational; no specific attacks are claimed and no contemporary figures are named.
keyClaims: Tawhid is the singular purpose for which all prophets were sent.
Hajj is the most concentrated ritual expression of tawhid.
Authentic tawhid requires active combat against 'polytheists' and 'tyrants', not worship alone.
Iran and the United States are the principal contemporary enemies of tawhid.
The group's armed campaign is the practical continuation of the prophetic mission.
significanceAssessment: A Hajj-timed editorial that fuses ritual obligation with operational mobilisation, consistent with al-Naba's recurring strategy of exploiting religious occasions for recruitment and justification of violence. The dual targeting of Iran and the United States signals continued two-front rhetorical posture rather than a tilt toward a single enemy. Thematic rather than operational; sets ideological frame rather than claiming specific activity.
notes: Single editorial page (page 3) only. Gregorian date converted from 12 Dhu al-Hijjah 1447 AH. Small-text passages in the central columns could not be read with full certainty, but core argument is clear and consistent across all readable sections.
